q-42494.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14226602/assets/2ee08e17ee0f474a675e83275c290a29a0f2814e5277694a5629282cfd861d56.png)

Find the polar coordinates for the intersection points of the circles $r=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $ and $r=\sqrt{3},$ shown above.
q-42494.worked_solution:
To determine the polar coordinates of the intersection points, we will solve the following system of equations for $r$ and $\theta :$  

$$
\{\begin{aligned}r=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ r=\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}
$$

We begin by setting the equations equal to each other and solve for $\theta .$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =\sqrt{3} \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this equation in the interval $[0,2\pi ),$ we obtain ${\theta }_{1}=\frac{4\pi }{3}$ and ${\theta }_{2}=\frac{5\pi }{3}$ .

Also, notice that $r=\sqrt{3}$ at both intersection points.

Therefore, polar coordinates of the points of intersection are 

$\,$ $(r,\theta )=(\sqrt{3},\frac{4\pi }{3})\,$ and $\,(r,\theta )=(\sqrt{3},\frac{5\pi }{3}).$

r=2−2sin⁡θr=1 We begin by setting the equations equal to each other and solve for θ. This gives 2−2sin⁡θ=12sin⁡θ=1sin⁡θ=12.

Solving this equation in the interval [0∘,360∘), we obtain θ1=30∘ and θ2=150∘.

Find the polar coordinates of the intersection points of the polar curves $r=3-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $ and $r=4+3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ shown above. Round your answers to $1$ decimal place where appropriate.
q-121827.worked_solution:
To determine the polar coordinates of the intersection points, we will solve the following system of equations for $r$ and $\theta :$  

$$
\{\begin{aligned}r=3-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ r=4+3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

We begin by setting the equations equal to each other and solve for $\theta .$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}3-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =4+3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ 5\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =-1 \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =-\frac{1}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this equation in the interval $[{0}^{∘},{360}^{∘}),$ we obtain ${\theta }_{1}≈{191.5}^{∘}$ and ${\theta }_{2}≈348.5,$ rounded to $1$ decimal place. 

Now, we use the equation $r=4+3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $ to find the $r$-coordinates of the intersection points: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{1} & =4+3\operatorname{sin}⁡{\theta }_{1}=4+3\cdot (-\frac{1}{5})=\frac{17}{5}=3.4 \\ {r}_{2} & =4+3\operatorname{cos}⁡{\theta }_{2}=4+3\cdot (-\frac{1}{5})=\frac{17}{5}=3.4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, polar coordinates of the points of intersection are

$\,$ $(r,\theta )≈(3.4,{191.5}^{∘})\,$ and $\,(r,\theta )≈(3.4,{348.5}^{∘}).$

$$
\{\begin{aligned}r=5-4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ r=1+4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \end{aligned}

q-121848.problem: The curves $r=2-3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $ and $r=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $ for $\theta \in [0,2\pi )$ intersect at a single point in the second quadrant. Determine the polar coordinates of this point.
q-121848.worked_solution:
To determine the polar coordinates of the intersection points, we will solve the following system of equations for $r$ and $\theta :$  

$$
\{\begin{aligned}r=2-3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ r=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

We begin by setting the equations equal to each other and solve for $\theta .$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}2-3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ 4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =2 \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this equation in the interval $[0,2\pi ),$ we obtain ${\theta }_{1}=\frac{\pi }{6}$ and ${\theta }_{2}=\frac{5\pi }{6}.$

Therefore, the $\theta $-coordinate of the point that we're interested in is $\theta =\frac{5\pi }{6},$ since it lies in the second quadrant.

Now, we use the equation $r=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $ to find the $r$-coordinate of our point:

$$
r=\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{5\pi }{6})=\frac{1}{2}
$$

Therefore, the polar coordinates of the desired intersection point are

$\,$ $(r,\theta )=(\frac{1}{2},\frac{5\pi }{6}).$
